paragraphs: Rabbotenu za"l aseru pat shel goyim, kede lehabdil otanu min haobede kokabim umazzalot (akku"m) betaklit hahebdel, shello nitareb venargil atzmenu immahem, sheal-yede zeh yimmasheku hallebabot veyiqrebu datam ellu leellu, veyabou liznut ulehitchatten immahem, ukemo sheera bearbot moab (bammidbar kh, -t).velo gazeru ella al pat shel chamishsha mine dagan, abal pat qitniyyot veshel orez vedochan, lo gazeru beelleh, mippene deenam chashuben, veen mebiin lide qarob daat: vegam en leaseram mishshum bishshule goyim, deen olin al shulchan melakim vesarim: deap-al-gab dehaorez oleh al shulchan melakim, haynu orez hambushshal biqdera, abal orez heasuy pat betannur, en oleh al shulchan melakim.

clarification.explanation: The Sages forbade gentile bread in order to distinguish us thoroughly from idolaters, so we would not mix and grow accustomed to them — since closeness draws hearts together and brings minds closer, which can lead to promiscuity and intermarriage with them, as happened in the plains of Moab. They decreed only against bread made from the five species of grain, but bread of legumes, rice, and millet was not forbidden, since these are not significant and do not lead to closeness of minds. Nor should they be forbidden under gentile cooking, since they do not grace the tables of kings and officials. And although cooked rice does grace the table of kings, this refers specifically to rice cooked in a pot, but rice made into bread in an oven does not grace the table of kings.
takeaways: The Sages forbade gentile bread to prevent closeness that leads to intermarriage.
The prohibition applies only to bread of the five grain species, not rice, millet, or legume bread.
Non-grain bread is not significant and also carries no gentile-cooking prohibition.
Rice cooked in a pot graces kings' tables, but rice bread does not.

paragraphs: Kesheggazeru rabbotenu za"l gezera zo shel pat, lo nitpashsheta bekol meqomot yisrael ella bepat baal-habbayit sheasao libne beto, abal bepat shel palter sheoseh limkor laacherim, lo nitpashshet haissur hazzeh bekol hammeqomot mippene haddechaq, dechayye haadam teluyim bepat: velaken yesh meqomot shennohagim hetter bepat palter bemaqom sheen pat yisrael, deen qarob daat kol kak, kevan sheoseq beummanuto. veyesh meqillin liqnot min palter goy apillu sheyyesh pat palter yisrael matzuy: veken nohagim poh irenu bagdad y" liqnot mippalter goy, ap-al-pi shemmatzuy pat palter yisrael. verabbenu haari"y za"l machmir apillu besapeq im hu mippalter yisrael o palter goy, ukemo shekkatab beshaar taame hammitzvot.

clarification.explanation: When the Sages decreed the prohibition of gentile bread, the decree did not extend everywhere, only to a homeowner's bread baked for his household's use. But a baker's bread, baked to sell to others, was not universally forbidden, due to the difficulty involved, since human life depends on bread. Therefore some places customarily permitted a gentile baker's bread where no Jewish bread is available, since there is not as much closeness involved, since the baker is simply engaged in his trade. Some are lenient to buy from a gentile baker even where a Jewish baker is available, and so was the Baghdad custom. But the Arizal was stringent even in doubt whether the bread came from a Jewish or gentile baker.
takeaways: The bread decree extended to a homeowner's bread, but was relaxed for a baker's bread due to necessity.
Some permit gentile bakery bread only when no Jewish bakery exists, and some even when one does.
In Baghdad, the custom was to buy from a gentile baker even when a Jewish baker was available.
The Arizal was stringent even in a case of doubt.

paragraphs: Lo haleku beissur zeh achar mi shehappat beyado akshav, ella achar haapiyya, lepikak pat baal-habbayit asura leolam, apillu qenaah palter, vaapillu shillechah leyisrael lebeto: veshel palter, mutteret leolam, apillu qenaah mimmennu baal-habbayit shehu goy. velaken haggoy zimmen et yisrael bebeto, vehebiu lo pat min palter goy, muttar leekol: veken im happalter goy zimmen et yisrael bebeto, vehebi lepanayv min happat sheasa limkor, hare zeh muttar leekol mimmennu: abal im hebi lo mehappat sheapa letzorek beto, hare zeh asur leekol mimmennu. veayyen "peri-chadash" seip-qatan yb: vahagam deharab "peri-toar" pelig, kebar hissigo harab "mizmor ledavid", veken iqqar.

clarification.explanation: In the prohibition of bread, one does not follow who currently holds the bread, but who baked it. Therefore a homeowner's bread is always forbidden, even if a gentile baker bought it and even if he sent it to a Jew's home. Whereas a baker's bread is always permitted, even if a gentile homeowner bought it from him. Therefore, if a gentile invited a Jew to his home and brought him bread he bought from a gentile baker, it is permitted to eat. Likewise, if the gentile baker himself invited a Jew to his home and served him from the bread he baked for sale, it is permitted. But if he served him from the bread he baked for his own household's use, it is forbidden to eat from it.
takeaways: The prohibition follows who baked it, not who currently holds it.
A homeowner's bread is always forbidden, even bought by a baker and sent to a Jew.
A baker's bread is always permitted, even bought by a gentile homeowner.
A baker who invites a Jew: permitted from sale bread, forbidden from his household bread.

paragraphs: Pat shel baale-battim, en lah hetter olamit, apillu bemaqom deeno matzuy pat yisrael vegam lo pat palter goy, deqayma lan kistam maran za"l deasar bepat shel baale-battim bekol gavna. vaapillu im yirtzeh lebashshelo lepat zeh leakelo al-yede bishshul, name asur, dela paqa issuro bekak.veayyen "keneset haggedola", haggahat hattur, ot ch, v"yosep ometz", siman t. vaapillu im hu besadeh sheen sham chashash chatnut, asur, vekannizkar b"bet-yosep": veayyen "qehal-yeuddeh" za"l. veen hetter lepat baale-battim ella beheka deaberu alayv shelosha yamim meet leet shello akal pat, o beshabbat mishshum oneg-shabbat: veayyen "peri-chadash" v"peri-toar" ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: A homeowner's bread has no leniency at all, even where neither Jewish bread nor gentile baker's bread is available, since we follow Maran, who forbade a homeowner's bread in every case. And even if one wishes to cook this bread and eat it that way, it is forbidden, since cooking does not remove its prohibition. Even if one is in a field where there is no concern of intermarriage, it is forbidden. There is no leniency for a homeowner's bread except where a full three days have passed with no bread eaten at all, or on the Sabbath for the sake of Sabbath delight.
takeaways: A homeowner's bread has no leniency ever, even with no other bread available.
Cooking the bread does not remove its prohibition.
Forbidden even in a field with no concern of intermarriage.
Leniency only after three full days with no bread at all, or on the Sabbath for Sabbath delight.

paragraphs: Yisreelim haholekim etzel haarbiyyim yoshebe ohalim, vesham en matzuy palter goy limkor – lo yokal min happat hammatzuy etzlam, shezzeh pat baal-habbayit veasur, ella yamtin ad shaa sheopin happat: ki ellu darkam leepot kol yom babboqer ubaereb, velipamim gam beemtza hayyom kesheyyizdammen etzlam orechim: veaz yannicha hayisrael qesam, dehaynu chatikat etz, betok hattannur, ubazeh makshir kol happat shebbattannur: sheen haddabar ella lihyot hekker dehappat shellahem asura. umeachar shebbachatikat etz echad shehinnicha yisrael, mosip chom meat battannur: vekol tosepet chom apillu meat, meqareb habbishshul have hekker bazeh: mihu, tzarik sheyyekavven shehu mesayyea bahatalat haqqesam kede lehakshir, abal im zaraq qesam lattannur kemitasseq bealema, shello kivven kede lehakshir la mehanne kelum: veayyen "keneset haggedola", haggahat habbet-yosep, ot kch v"qehal-yeuddeh" za"l.

clarification.explanation: Jews who visit Arab tent-dwellers, where there is no gentile baker selling bread, should not eat from the bread found among them, which is homeowner's bread and forbidden, but should wait until baking time, since their custom is to bake every day, morning and evening, and sometimes even midday when guests happen to arrive. Then the Jew should place a splinter — that is, a piece of wood — inside the oven, thereby validating all the bread in the oven. Since any addition of heat, even a small one, hastens the baking and is effective, the main point being that there is a distinguishing mark that gentile bread is forbidden. But one must intend, in placing the splinter, to validate the bread; if he threw a splinter into the oven as an incidental act without intent to validate it, it accomplishes nothing.
takeaways: Among tent-dwellers with no baker, a Jew should wait for baking time.
Placing a splinter in the oven validates all the bread in it.
Any added heat hastens the baking and is effective, the key being a distinguishing mark.
One must intend to validate; an incidental, unintentional act accomplishes nothing.

paragraphs: Yisrael shemmebi goy lebeto leepot lo betannur shello yizzaharu bene habbayit litten beyadam bitchillat hesseq shel hattannur agudda achat shel etzim, veaz haggoy gomer hahesseq veopeh: veyesh lismok al hattalat haetzim shehetilu beyadam beappeh rishona, dehaynu shemmemalle et hattannur pat verodeh oto, veken baapiyya sheniyya, shechozer umemalle hattannur pat verodeh: ki koach hassaqa shellahem odenna battannur baapiyya hashsheniyya abal achar zeh, tzarik sheyyachzeru veyannichu etzim beyadam kede lemallot hattannur pat beappeh hashshelishit, veken al zo hadderek.

clarification.explanation: A Jew who brings a gentile into his home to bake for him in his oven — the household members should be careful to hand the gentile one bundle of wood at the start of firing the oven, and then the gentile finishes firing and bakes. One may rely on the wood handed to him for the first baking, that is, filling the oven with bread and removing it, and likewise for the second baking, refilling and removing it, since the strength of the Jew's firing still remains in the oven for the second baking. But afterward, wood must again be handed to him for filling the oven for the third baking, and so on.
takeaways: A Jew bringing a gentile to bake in his oven should hand him a bundle of wood at the start of firing.
The firing's strength validates the first and second bakings.
For the third baking, wood must again be handed to him, and so on.

paragraphs: Pat shel yisrael sheapaah haggoy, velo hinnicha hayisrael qesam velo chayeta baesh, hare zeh asur kedin pat baal-habbayit goy, veasur leakelo leyisrael. ella yachtekennu lachatikot veyimkerennu legoy, deen yisrael qonim miggoy chatikot pat: abal asur lemakero belo chittuk, shemma yimkerennu haggoy leyisrael acher al yede palter. veim hem mesuppaqim baddabar, im naasa heksher lattannur al-yede yisrael o lav, hare zeh muttar, desapeqa derabbanan lequlla, vekannizkar bashsha"k v"peri chadash".

clarification.explanation: A Jew's bread baked by a gentile, without the Jew placing a splinter or stoking the fire, is forbidden like a gentile homeowner's bread, and a Jew may not eat it. Rather, he should cut it into pieces and sell it to a gentile, since Jews do not buy bread pieces from a gentile. But it is forbidden to sell it uncut, lest the gentile resell it to another Jew as though from a baker. And if there is doubt whether the oven was validated by a Jew, it is permitted, since a doubt in a rabbinic matter is resolved leniently.
takeaways: A Jew's bread baked by a gentile without validation is forbidden like homeowner's bread.
It should be sold to a gentile in cut pieces, since Jews do not buy bread pieces.
It is forbidden to sell it uncut, lest it be resold to a Jew.
Doubt about oven validation is resolved leniently (a rabbinic doubt).

paragraphs: Hammoshelim shennotenim bekol yom pat lamsharetim o laropeim yisreelim, hare zeh kepat palter, ken katab mhryq"sh za"l, vehiskimu bazeh kamma gedole haacharonim, veap-al-pi sheharab ha"keneset haggedola" oser haiqqar kisbarat hammattirim: veayyen "shiyyure-beraka", ot v. mihu, harab mhryq"sh za"l lo hittir ella bikhay gavna, shehem notenim lo happat beyado laasot bo mah sheyyirtzeh, leakelo o lemakero, ki dabar zeh alehem betorat choq, latet kol yom pat qatzub leellu : abal yisrael shebba oreach lebet haggoy, veapu lo pat baaburo, vehebiu lepanayv davqa, ki hem kebar akelu ap-al-pi shello apu ella baaburo, en zeh chashib kepat palter, ella pat shel baal habbayit veasur: veen lomar, kevan denotenim oto lo bechinnam, chashib kemeker, deha iqqar gezerat chaza"l al oreach hammitareach etzlam, vekol oreach okel bechinnam. veadderabba, kevan deapu baaburo likbodo, yesh qarob daat vachashash chatnut tepe: laken kol heka shemmebiim lepanayv betorat seuda lisod, ap-al-pi shehem kebar akelu, velo apu zeh happat ella bishbilo, hare zeh niqra pat baal-habbayit veasur, veda ki harab "zekor leabraham", cheleq , ot poAdonai lamad middin mhryq"sh za"l hannizkar hetter, beheka deopeh haggoy bishbil yisrael latet lo happat tzeda ladderek, ayyen sham: veetzli en hetter hazzeh barur adayin.

clarification.explanation: Rulers who give a fixed daily bread ration to Jewish servants or physicians — this bread has the law of a baker's bread and is permitted, as Maharikash wrote and the great later authorities agreed, although the Knesset HaGedolah forbids it. But this leniency applies specifically when the bread is given into his hand to do with as he wishes, to eat or to sell, since it is their fixed obligation to give a daily bread ration. But a Jew who comes as a guest to a gentile's home, and bread was baked for him specifically and served for him to eat, even though the household itself has already eaten — this is not like a baker's bread but a homeowner's bread, and is forbidden. And one cannot say that since it is given free, it is like a sale, since the essence of the decree was stated regarding a guest being hosted, and every guest eats for free — on the contrary, since it was baked specifically for his honor, there is even greater closeness and concern of intermarriage. Know that Rabbi "Zachur LeAvraham" derived from the aforementioned Maharikash ruling a leniency specifically in a case where the gentile bakes bread for a Jew to give him as provisions for the road, not to eat immediately in front of him, but the author of the Ben Ish Chai writes that this leniency is still not clear to him.
takeaways: A fixed daily bread ration given to Jewish servants has the law of baker's bread — permitted.
This applies only when given into his hand to do as he wishes.
Bread baked specifically for a Jewish guest's honor is homeowner's bread — forbidden.
Being given free does not make it a sale; being baked for his honor increases the concern of closeness.
Some derive a leniency for bread baked as travel provisions, but the Ben Ish Chai remains unresolved on this.

paragraphs: Dabar shebbishshelo goy, apillu beshello bebet yisrael ubikli shel yisrael, asaruhu chaza"l mishshum chatnut: veod yesh bazeh taam acher: shemma yargil yisrael leekol min tabshilehem, veyaakilehu dabar tame: ak lo asur chaza"l bebishshule goyim, ella bedabar sheeno neekol kemo shehu chay: vegam od tenay sheni sheyyihyeh oto dabar rauy laalot al shulchan melakim lelappet bo happat o leqinnucha seuda, o betorat maakol, veap-al-pi sheeno neekol betorat liptan: uben im nishtanna mibberiyyato al-yede habbishshul, ben im lo nishtanna, ella nikkar adayin leachar habbishshul kemo battechilla hare zeh asur mishshum bishshule haggoyim. veha debaenan oleh al shulchan melakim - lav davqa melakim, ella apillu al shulchan sarim shebbeeretz hahi, name asur: veayyen "shiyyure-beraka", ot b, ushear acharonim: veken sabar rabbenu haari"y za"l.

clarification.explanation: Something cooked by a gentile, even cooked in a Jew's house and Jew's vessel, was forbidden by the Sages due to intermarriage, and an additional reason — lest a Jew grow accustomed to eating their dishes and be fed something impure. But they forbade gentile cooking only for something not eaten raw as it is, with the additional condition that it be fit to grace the table of kings, to accompany bread, as a dessert, or as a dish. Whether the item changed from its natural state through cooking or did not change and is still recognizable as before, it is forbidden under gentile cooking. And regarding the requirement that it grace the table of kings, the intent is not specifically kings, but even what graces the table of that land's officials is forbidden.
takeaways: Something cooked by a gentile is forbidden even in a Jew's house and vessel, due to intermarriage.
The prohibition applies only to something not eaten raw, and fit for kings' or officials' tables.
Applies whether or not the item's natural state changed through cooking.
"Kings' table" includes even the officials of that land.

paragraphs: Haorez - ap-al-pi shehappat shello muttar kidkatabnu leel, mikkol maqom orez shebbishshelo goy, asur, mishshum deorez mebushshal hu oleh al shulchan melakim: vaapillu bimqoman sheen darkam lelappet bo et happat, mikkol maqom hu oleh betorat maakol. vehakkemehin sheqqorin bearbi "kime" (sug pitriyya betzurat tpv"), asurin bebishshul, mishshum deolin hem al shulchan melakim vesarim: abal mah sheqqorin bearbi "apteyyr"(pitriyyat geshem metzuya), en bahem bishshule goyim, deen olin al shulchan melakim. vehashshumin, yesh bahem issur bishshule goyim: veayyen "peri-chadash".

clarification.explanation: Rice, although its bread is permitted as explained, nevertheless rice cooked by a gentile is forbidden, since cooked rice graces the table of kings. And even where it is not their custom to accompany bread with it, it still graces the table as a dish on its own. Truffles, called in Arabic "kima," are forbidden under gentile cooking, since they grace the tables of kings and officials. But those called "aftir," which are common rain mushrooms, carry no gentile-cooking prohibition, since they do not grace kings' tables. And garlic carries the prohibition of gentile cooking.
takeaways: Cooked rice by a gentile is forbidden even though rice bread is permitted.
Significant truffles are forbidden under gentile cooking.
Common rain mushrooms carry no such prohibition.
Garlic carries the gentile-cooking prohibition.

paragraphs: Betza ap-al-pi sherauy legameah chayya im bishshelah goy, asura: veim bishshelah yisrael battechilla apillu kol- dehu vesilleqa, veachar-kak leqachah goy ugemar bishshul, muttar.

clarification.explanation: An egg, even though fit to be gulped raw, if cooked by a gentile is forbidden under gentile cooking, since most people eat it cooked. But if a Jew began cooking it first, even a little, and set it aside, and then a gentile took it and finished cooking it, it is permitted, since a Jew already began it.
takeaways: A cooked egg by a gentile is forbidden even though it can be eaten raw.
If a Jew began cooking it even slightly and a gentile finished it, it is permitted.

paragraphs: Apunim sheqqorin bearbe "chometz" (chumus) shiqlo otam haggoyim katab rabbenu harab chayyim veyittol za"l beshaar taame hammitzvot, parashat eqeb, beshem rabbenu haari"y za"l, daasurim middina, lepi deellu haqqelayot shellahem olin al shulchan melakim vesarim shel otam hammeqomot sheosin otam haqqelayot, ayyen sham. umiddebarayv mashma deoser otam gam bemaqom sheen olin al shulchan melakim o sarim, mippene shebbemaqom sheosin otam olin. veayyen "chayyim shaal", cheleq , siman ad, ot v, shechaqar bazeh, vesop dabar dato nata leesor gam bemaqom sheen olin. veod katab rabbenu harab chayyim veyittol za"l sham, dehatturmosin hannishlaqin al yede haggoyim, muttarim middina, deen olin al shulchan melakim: veraq hizhir rabbenu haari"y za"l shello leakelam mittorat chumera davqa. veod katab sham deen lishtot qum hechalab achar shenniqpeh hechalab venibdal hammayim mimmennu, ukemo shekkatab morenu rabbi eliezer mimmitz za"l, ayyen sham.

clarification.explanation: Regarding chickpeas, called in Arabic "hummus," roasted by gentiles, the Arizal wrote they are forbidden by law, since their roasted form graces the tables of kings and officials in the places where they are made. His words imply he forbids them even in a place where they do not grace kings' tables there, since they do grace such tables in the place where they are made. The Chida also leaned toward forbidding them even in a place where they do not grace such tables. The Arizal further wrote that lupine beans parboiled by gentiles are permitted by law, since they do not grace kings' tables, and he only warned not to eat them as a matter of stringency. He also wrote that one should not drink the whey ("qom") remaining after milk curdles and the water separates from it.
takeaways: Roasted chickpeas by a gentile are forbidden, since they grace kings' tables in the places they are made.
The Chida leaned toward forbidding even where they do not grace such tables locally.
Parboiled lupine beans are permitted by law, though the Arizal warned against them as a stringency.
One should not drink the whey remaining after milk curdles.

paragraphs: Haqqitniyyot sheqqorin bearbe "beaqyali" (sheuit metzuya) im hem qeluyim, muttarim, deen haqqeluyim olin al shulchan melakim o sarim, abal hashsheluqin asurim, deolin al shulchan melakim o sarim. utemarim hammarim qetzat, sheenam neekalim ella al-yede haddechaq im bishshelam goy, asurim.

clarification.explanation: The legume called in Arabic "baqilli" (beans), if roasted, is permitted, since roasted beans do not grace the tables of kings and officials, but boiled beans are forbidden, since they do grace kings' and officials' tables. And slightly bitter dates, eaten only under difficulty, if cooked by a gentile are forbidden, since something eaten raw only under difficulty still carries the prohibition of gentile cooking.
takeaways: Roasted beans are permitted; boiled beans are forbidden, since they grace kings' tables.
Bitter dates eaten raw only with difficulty, if cooked by a gentile, are forbidden.
Something eaten raw only under difficulty still carries the gentile-cooking prohibition.

paragraphs: Hallepet sheqqorin beereb "shellogem" (lepet lebana), veken lepet haadom sheqqorin "shpndr" (seleq adom), yesh bahem issur bishshule goyim, dehem olin al shulchan melakim o sarim: veap-al-pi sheyyesh qetzat bene-adam deokelim otam chayyim - batela datam: veayyen "peri chadash", seip qatan kd. vekol zeh bishluqim o mebushshalim biqdera, abal hatztzeluyan beeper cham sheqqorin "male" (remetz), ap-al-pi shennaasa bahem taam tob, im kol zeh, mechamat shehem meluklakim beeper, vehu dabuq bahem vei epshar lehitqanneach mechamat shehu dabuq belichlucha shebbahem, al-ken en olim al shulchan melakim vesarim, demeisi lehu. veen lomar deyiqlepum vaybium lipnehem: chada, dei epshar shello yidbaq eper betok shellahem: veod, apillu im epshar lehizzaher bahem lehaabir hallikluk meal hattok shellahem en rauy hattok shellahem lebaddo bihyoto bipne atzmo lekabbed bo melakim o sarim: veod, mechamat shehu lach, yimas baachizatam bo lebaddo.

clarification.explanation: The white turnip called "shalgam," and likewise the red beet called "span-dar," carry the prohibition of gentile cooking, since they grace the tables of kings and officials. And although a few people eat them raw, their view is nullified relative to most of the world. All this applies when boiled or cooked in a pot, but if roasted in hot ash (embers), even though this gives them good flavor, since they become soiled with clinging ash that cannot be cleaned off, they do not grace kings' and officials' tables, being repulsive, and carry no gentile-cooking prohibition. And one cannot say to peel them, since it is impossible for ash not to stick to their interior as well, and the interior alone is also not fit to honor kings.
takeaways: Cooked white turnip and red beet by a gentile are forbidden, since they grace kings' tables.
The minority who eat them raw is nullified relative to most of the world.
Roasted in hot ash, they become repulsive and do not grace kings' tables, carrying no prohibition.
Peeling does not help, since ash sticks to the interior too, which alone is not fit for kings.

paragraphs: Supganin shel goyim shebbelilatam rakka, veneepa al-yede mashqeh lav nahma hu, vaasurin mishshum bishshule goyim: veayyen "peri chadash", v"shiyyure-beraka", veken ha"zlby" sheqqorin beirenu "zngvl" (mematteq miqqemach vesukkar metugganim), asura mishshum bishshule goyim lekulle alema: vehammattir otah, hu mishshum dela sayyemuha qama lemaaseh shellah, ki beemet en hepresh benah leben hassupganin: veayyen "shiyyure-beraka", ot yg.

clarification.explanation: Gentile doughnuts made of a soft batter and fried with a liquid are not considered bread and are forbidden under gentile cooking, and cannot be permitted through oven validation like bread. Likewise "zalabiya," called in Baghdad "zangula," a sweet of fried flour and sugar, is forbidden under gentile cooking according to all opinions, since there is no difference between it and doughnuts.
takeaways: Soft-batter doughnuts fried with liquid are not bread and are forbidden under gentile cooking, not validated by oven-firing.
"Zangula," a fried flour-and-sugar sweet, is likewise forbidden under gentile cooking according to all.
Their law is that of gentile cooking, not bread.

paragraphs: Haqqeho shemmebashshelin haggoyim yesh oserin veyesh mattirin. umaran rabbenu haari"y za"l asar otah: ak en beyadenu limchot beyad hammeqillim sheyyesh lahem al mah lismok, ubiprat bemaqom sheppashat hamminhag lehattir. upoh irenu bagdad hamminhag pashut miqqodem qadmeta lishtot qhvv shel goyim apillu bammaqom hannoad shellah: ubevadday baal-nepesh tzarik lehachmir: vehatztzenuin, moshekin yedehem mimmenna, beram, apillu adam chashub, im holek lebet goyim gedolim laasot "vezeta"(biqqur nimusin) mukrach hu lishtot mikkamma sibbot sheyyesh bahem taam.

clarification.explanation: Regarding coffee cooked by gentiles, some forbid it under gentile cooking and some permit it, and the Arizal forbade it. But we cannot protest against the lenient, who have grounds to rely upon, especially where the lenient custom has spread. In Baghdad the plain, long-standing custom is to drink gentile coffee, even at its place of sale. Certainly one who is scrupulous with himself should be stringent, and the modest keep their hands away from it. Nevertheless, even an important person, if visiting the home of important gentiles for a courtesy visit, is compelled to drink it for several reasons.
takeaways: Gentile-cooked coffee is disputed; the Arizal forbade it, others are lenient.
One cannot protest the lenient, especially where the custom has spread, as in Baghdad.
One who is scrupulous should be stringent; the modest avoid it.
Even an important person visiting gentiles for courtesy is compelled to drink it for several reasons.

paragraphs: Chittim sheshsholeqin otam haggoyim tzache bishshul ad shemmaggiim lemaakal ben derusay, vechozerin umeyabbeshim otam, vezehu sheqqorin bearbe "bvrg'vl", muttar liqnoto min haggoyim kede lebashshelo uleokelo, debishshul haggoyim eno chashub kelum, kevan denityabbesh vetu la chazi, ukemo shekkatab maran za"l beshu"t "abqat- rokel", siman l. veayyen "shiyyure-beraka" v"erek hashshulchan", veken hamminhag pashut poh irenu bagdad,.vekatab "erek-hashshulchan", deim naasa "burgul" al-yede yisrael, ubishshelo haggoy sheni en lo hetter mitztzad bishshul rishon shebbishshel yisrael. vehinneh poh irenu yesh peri chimmutz beyoter sheqqorin oto "dibdayeb" (peri hadar chimmutz mar, baal qelippa aba shimmushit), vehu kemo etrogin, umebashshelin qelippato heabeh besukkar, yesh bazeh issur bishshule goyim, yaan deim mebashshel achar shennityabbesh, enah neekelet apillu al-yede haddechaq; veim mebashshel beodah lacha, deneekelet al-yede haddechaq, hinneh anan qayma lan kemaran za"l disbira leh: neekol chay al-yede haddechaq, yesh bo bishshule goyim. veken peri sheqqorin "nryng'h" (peri hadar chimmutz-mar, "chush-chash"), beodam qetannim harbeh, hem marim kelaana, umebashshelim otam besukkar, yesh bazeh issur bishshule goyim, deen neekalim chayyim apillu al-yede haddechaq. veken mirqachat sheqqorin bearbe "sekengebin" (ribat haddarim), shehu chimmutz shel peri limon chimmutz shemmebashshelim oto besukkar, ap-al-pi shenneekol al-yede haddechaq qodem bishshul, yesh bo bishshule goyim kisbarat maran za"l hannizkeret.

clarification.explanation: Wheat that gentiles parboil slightly until reaching the measure of "Ben Drosai" food, and then dry again — called in Arabic "burghul" — is permitted to buy from gentiles in order to cook and eat, since the gentile's cooking is considered nothing once it has dried and is unfit for eating as is. But if the burghul was made by a Jew and then cooked by a second gentile, it has no leniency from the Jew's initial cooking. In Baghdad there is a very sour fruit called "dabdib," whose thick peel is cooked in sugar, and this carries the prohibition of gentile cooking, since if cooked after drying it is not eaten even under difficulty, and if cooked while still moist it is eaten under difficulty — and we follow Maran that something eaten raw only under difficulty carries the gentile-cooking prohibition. Likewise the fruit called "naranja" while small and bitter, cooked in sugar, carries the gentile-cooking prohibition, since it is not eaten raw even under difficulty. Likewise the preserve called in Arabic "sikanjabin," a citrus jam made from sour lemon cooked in sugar — even though it was eaten under difficulty before cooking — carries the gentile-cooking prohibition, following Maran's aforementioned view.
takeaways: Burghul (parboiled and dried wheat) is permitted to buy from gentiles, since drying nullifies the cooking.
Burghul made by a Jew and cooked by a gentile has no leniency from the Jew's initial preparation.
The sour fruit "dabdib" cooked in sugar is forbidden under gentile cooking.
Small bitter "naranja" cooked in sugar is forbidden, not eaten raw even under difficulty.
Lemon preserve "sikanjabin" cooked in sugar is forbidden, following Maran's view.

paragraphs: En habarat tannur moelet ella bepat, abal bishar debarim hammitbashshelim, eno moil ella hahannacha al haesh, o sheyyaaseh hayisrael shear tzareke bishshul, kegon sheyyehapek veyannicha beopen shebbelo zeh lo haya mitbashshel.veap-al-gab deyesh omerim degam bebishshul mehanne kedin pat anan batar maran za"l geriran, sheppasaq leesor, vegam bediabad yesh lehachmir: veayyen "peri chadash" ushear acharonim, vaapillu ledaat hammattirim bechittuy zeh eno ella-im-ken choteh begechalim qodem shehiggia lemaakal ben derusay, vegam shehayeta beopen dehachittuy hahu moil lehosip habbishshul, vekannizkar baacharonim za"l. veha dimhanne hahannacha al haesh ledidan, haynu davqa im hinnichah bemaqom sherauy lehitbashshel shelish bishshulo shehu shiur maakal bin-derusay: veim lav, yesh leesor gam bediabad. velaken im hinnicha yisrael habbasar o haqqedera al gechalim omemot sheen rauy lehitbashshel shelish bishshulo: veqodem shennitbashshel shelish, ba haggoy vesilleqa mishsham vehinnichah bipnim yoter, hare zeh asur, deha nitbattela maaseh yisrael qodem shennitbashshel shelish bishshulo.

clarification.explanation: A Jew's firing of the oven helps validate only bread, but for other cooked items it does not help; rather the Jew himself must place the item on the fire, or perform another act of the cooking process, such as turning the food in a manner without which it would not cook. Although some say firing helps for cooking too, like bread, we follow Maran, who forbids this, and even after the fact one should be stringent. A Jew's placement on the fire helps only if he placed the item where it would cook at least a third of its cooking, the measure of "Ben Drosai" food; if not, one should forbid it even after the fact. Therefore, if a Jew placed meat or a pot on dying coals not hot enough to cook a third, and before it cooked a third a gentile came and moved it further in, this is forbidden, since the Jew's action was nullified before a third was cooked.
takeaways: A Jew's oven-firing validates only bread; other cooking requires the Jew's own placement on the fire or an essential cooking act.
We follow Maran, who forbids relying on firing alone for cooking, even after the fact.
The Jew's placement helps only if it reaches a third of the cooking ("Ben Drosai").
If a gentile moves it further in before a third is cooked, it is forbidden.

paragraphs: Otam hambashshelim dagim bepurin (tannur apiyya gadol, baal mishshetach meozen) shel goy, tzarik sheyyannicha yisrael et haqqeara shehaddag betokah bazeh happurin al haesh, bemaqom sheshsham titbashshel, vela saggi lehaknisah meat al-yede yisrael, vehaggoy yidchop otah lehaknisah bammaqom harauy; veim asa ken, haddag asur mishshum bishshule goyim. veken kesheosin "bqlvv", shehu reqiqin daqqin asuyin miqqemach hannillosh bechema, umannichim betokam sukkar veluzim ketushim umannichim otam baqqeara, umaknisin otah betok happurni, shetztzarik sheyyaknisah yisrael veyannichenna bemaqom harauy, velo yesirenna haggoy; ki zeh en lo din apiyya battannur, ella din bishshule goyim, dezeh eno neepa ella mitbashshel.

clarification.explanation: Those who cook fish in a gentile's large baking oven ("furin") must have the Jew himself place the dish containing the fish on the fire where it will cook, and it does not suffice for him to insert it slightly and have the gentile push it to the proper place — if done this way, the fish is forbidden under gentile cooking. Likewise, when making "baklava" — thin sheets of dough kneaded with butter, with sugar and crushed nuts, placed in a dish inside the oven — the Jew must insert and place it in the proper spot himself, without the gentile moving it, since this has the law not of oven-baking but of gentile cooking, since this is not baked but cooked.
takeaways: Cooking fish in a gentile's oven requires the Jew himself to place the dish in the proper cooking spot.
It is not enough to insert it slightly and let the gentile push it further.
Baklava has the law of cooking, not baking, requiring the same Jewish placement.

paragraphs: Ap-al-gab deqayma lan: malucha o kabush, hare hu kimbushshal, mikkol maqom beissur bishshule goyim lo gazeru al hammalucha vehakkabush, velaken im melach o kabash haggoy, muttar: vehu haddin hamushshan, sheim bishshelo haggoy al-yede ishshun, muttar, yaan ki hamushshan kedin bishshule goyim hu baya betalmud yerushalmi dela ippeshita, vekivvun debishshule goyim hu midderabbanan pasequ happoseqim lehattir, ukemo shekkatab harab hammaggid za"l, veken katab "pene-mosheh" bebeur hayyerushalmi: vaayin "matteh-yosep", yoreh dea, siman z, ot , v"machaziq beraka", yoreh dea, siman pz, ot yb, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Although we hold that a salted or pickled item has the law of a cooked one, nevertheless regarding the prohibition of gentile cooking, the Sages did not decree against salted or pickled items, and therefore if a gentile salted or pickled it, it is permitted. The same applies to a smoked item — if a gentile "cooked" it by way of smoking, it is permitted, since the law of a smoked item regarding gentile cooking remains a doubt in the Jerusalem Talmud, and since gentile cooking is rabbinic, the authorities ruled leniently.
takeaways: The Sages did not decree gentile cooking against salted or pickled items — permitted.
A smoked item by a gentile is likewise permitted.
The law of a smoked item remains a doubt in the Jerusalem Talmud, resolved leniently since gentile cooking is rabbinic.

paragraphs: Kol dabar malucha shenneekol al-yede melichato, kegon dagim qetannim vekayyotze, im achar melichato nitbashshel o nitzla al-yede haggoy, en bazeh issur bishshule goyim. abal hamushshan shebbishshelo haggoy, aseru maran za"l b"bet-yosep", vehaacharonim hittiru.

clarification.explanation: Anything salted that is eaten by virtue of its salting alone, such as small fish and the like, if a gentile cooked or roasted it after salting, carries no gentile-cooking prohibition, since it was already fit to eat through the salting. But a smoked item cooked by a gentile — Maran forbade it in Beit Yosef, while the later authorities permitted it.
takeaways: Something already edible through salting, later cooked or roasted by a gentile, carries no gentile-cooking prohibition.
A smoked item cooked by a gentile — Maran forbade it, but later authorities permitted it.

paragraphs: Hassoker sheqqorin qn"d (gebishe sukkar sheqop) sheosin oto beare eroppa min hallepet haadom "y bishshul, nitorer bazeh haggaon shem aryeh za"l mishshum issur bishshule goyim. dehallepet eno neekol chay ella "y haddechaq, veqayma lan apillu neekol "y haddechaq yesh bo bishshule goyim. venitztaer meod al haddabar, shehu tzarik lekol adam, velo matza lo taam barur behetter shello, kaasher yireh roeh besipro yeuyyan sham. vaana abda matzati lo hetter barur beezrat Adonai yitbarek, vehinni koteb taame hahetter beqitztzur vah' yaazor li. vehu, ki haggaon za"l sham besiman k"b hebi open maaseh hassoker hannizkar, ki mehayyora asher al haach yatza hahebel el hayyora harishona asher sham hammitz vehammohal, erek y"ch gerad (maalot chom). veaach"k yored hammohel likli sheni, vegam sham yabo hahebel derek qanim arbaim gerad. veaach"k yored lakkeli hashshelishi, vesham hahebel shemonim gerad, vesham gemar bishshulo, ad kan leshono. nimtza lepi zeh, hahebel hambashshel et hammitz eno naaseh miggup haesh shemmadliq haggoy, ella haggoy madliq esh tachat hayyora lechammem hammayim shebbetokah, umin chimmum hammayim hannaaseh mikkocho shel goy nolad hahebel. nimtza hahebel hu koach kocho shel haggoy, veachar shennaasa hahebel veala baqqanim lo yesh baqqaneh mitz kede lehitbashshel, ella hahebel netaq meelayv min haqqaneh veyored letok hayyora asher betokah hammitz, vesham mebashshelo meat bishshul sheeno rauy laakila. veaach"k chozer hammitz venishpak min yoreh zo el yoreh shenit, vegam hahebel netaq gam ken miyyoreh zo derek haqqanim veyored layyora hashshenit umebashshel sham hammitz. vaadayin lo gamar bishshulo, ad shechozer venishpak hammitz layyora hashshelishit. vegam hahebel oleh derek haqqanim min hashshenit el hashshelishit, vesham yihyeh gemar bishshulo. nimtza lepi zeh, apillu bishshul harishon shel hammitz beyora rishona, nechshab zeh hahebel shemmebashshelo sham koach shelishi, ki hachimmum hu koach rishon, vehahebel hannolad venaasa mikkoach chimmum hammayim hu koach sheni, viridato layyora harishona shel hammitz hu koach shelishi. veken hammitz atzmo shel happeri, en haggoy mesimo beyadayim bayyora shemmitbashshel bah, ella netaq veyotze mikkeli el keli al yede kochot shel galgallim. ki battechilla qodem heto betok hayyora shemmitbashshel bah mannichim oto bikli lerachatzu, veaach"k netaq meoto hakkeli likli acher "y haggalgal kede lepirko, veaach"k netaq likli acher "y galgal kede laasoto mitz, veaach"k netaq "y galgal venishpak layyora shehu mitbashshel bah beoto hahebel. vehadderek hu sheyyabi haggoy retzua hatteluya baggalgal haggadol, veyiqsherenna baggalgal shehu tachat oto hakkeli shebbetoko hammitz, veaz "y tenuat haggalgal yaggia haggalgal lazeh hakkeli shebbo hammitz sheyyihyeh meriq et hammitz shebbetoko layyora shehu mitbashshel bah. venimtza zeh hammitz lo sam oto haggoy beyadayim betok hayyora shel habbishshul, ella ba lesham "y shelosha kochot, shehem: haretzua, vehaggalgal shehenia et hakkeli shebbo hammitz, vehakkeli atzmo sheheriq et hammitz layyora. vahare gam bazeh yesh shelosha kochot, keinyan galgal veqora veluchot hannizkarim (besiman qk"h).

Vehinneh (besiman qy"g) katab maran za"l bb"y: matzati katub (hu mahari"l) dinpich bappeh moil bebishshule goyim, dachashib kegupo, ureaya mippereq ketzad haregel mittarnegol shettaqa bikle zekukit veku', umashma middebarayv dehu haddin lenopeach bemappucha o bishpoperet, ad kan debarayv ayyen sham. vehinneh bevadday mappucha ushepoperet en koach kocho, ella chashib deharucha hayyotze min hammappucha hu koach yado, veken harucha hayyotze min hashshepoperet hu yotze mippiv. venimtzenu lemedin mikkan dekocho kegupo leinyan bishshule goyim. abal koach kocho yesh lomar deeno oser bebishshule goyim, vekol shekken bekoach kocho deikka shelosha kochot devadday muttar. veayyen minchat yaaqob bitshubot siman l"v mah shekkatab bedin nopeach qesam mibbeged ishto nidda, yeuyyan sham. umah shekkatab mera"n za"l bedin yen nesek si' qk"h seip b' dekoach kocho kegupo dame veraq im hu koach koach kocho sheyyesh shelosha kochot muttar bediabad apillu bishtiyya vekatebu happoseqim dilkattechilla apillu baasara kochot asur yeuyyan sham yesh lemor shane yayin shehu mishshum derek aboda zara hechmiru beh degam koach kocho asur: vehinneh beharamba"m za"l pereq t"v mehilkot shabbat halaka y"ch pasaq kocho birshut harabbim aseru chakamim vekocho bekarmelit lo aseru ak koach kocho muttar apillu birshut harabbim yeuyyan sham velikora qasheh middin shabbat atzmo depasaq haramba"m za"l dehannopeach chayyab mishshum mabir venireh letaretz bs"d deqayma lan kol meleket shabbat mimmishkan gamerinan kol midde dela hava kevateh bammishkan eno chayyab alayv min hattora vehinneh nopeach baesh hava bammishkan devadday hayu nopechin lehabir haesh laken qayma lan nopeach chayyab mishshum mabir ak keshemmotziin mereshut lirshut hayu motziin beyadam velo bekoach uzeriqa "g dahavaya hatam hinneh zo chashiba kegupo veen zeh chashib kocho velaken kevan dela have inyan kocho birshuyot lemashken en issur bekocho min hattora birshut harabbim ella midderabbanan abal bekarmelit shehi iqqarah midderabbanan lo gazeru velaken koach kocho gam birshut harabbim muttar umah sheaseru beyayin koach kocho mukrach lomar kidkatebina dibyayin hechmiru topi mishshum serek aboda zara deha matzinu sheasu bo kamma chumrat shello hechmiru bahem bishar issurin derabbanan: veraiti lemaran za"l beshulchano hattahor siman r" seip t"l im haya rokeb al behema venizdallepu mayim beragle habbehema lo pesaluhu ayyen sham veraiti leharab debar mosheh beyoreh dea siman k"d dap m"t ammud d' shekkatab tamo shel maran za"l mishshum dehave koach kocho velaken kasher veim ken mizzeh yesh lilmod dekoach kocho la have kegupo ak achar hayyishshub deayyete deen hekreach lomar hattaam mishshum dekoach kocho lav kegupo kemo shekkatab harab debar mosheh za"l. ubedin hashshechita beyoreh dea (si' g') pasaq maran za"l kocho kegupo veraiti lehaggaon tebuat shor seip qatan d' dimsappeqa leh bekoach kocho i have kegupo o lav yeuyyan sham amenam harab debar mosheh za"l hannizkar leel peshita leh dekoach kocho lav kegupo umeparesh tama demaran behaki gam harab zikron yosep za"l beyoreh dea siman y"g dap m' "g peshita leh dekoach kocho lav kegupo yeuyyan sham abal vadday yesh lanu lomar dehaggaon tebuot shor za"l hannizkar lo nistappeq ella bekoach kocho abal bishlosha kochot peshita leh dela have kegupo.

Ulepi zeh beniddon didan dehave shelosha kochot veyoter la chashib zeh bishshul shel goy umuttar lekulle alema. veod ha it lan reaya atzuma min hayyayin desiman qk"h d"g dehechmiru beh tepe pasaq maran debishlosha kochot muttar bediabad apillu bishtiyya veniddon didan hu diabad shezzeh hassoker hu kebar naaseh bayyad goyim vahare zeh muttar gamur beli shum piqpuq.

Veod ani roeh bs"d detaam hahetter shekkatab harab abraham yaaqob za"l shehebio haggaon shem aryeh besiman k"b hu taam chashub sherauy lismok alayv dekatab shezzeh eno mitbashshel baesh ella raq behebel ukemo sheameru en bamushshan issur bishshule goyim ken yesh lomar behebel ad kan debarayv umah sheddacha harab hamchabber taam zeh bishte yadayim hinneh bimchilat kebodo lo daq demah sheameru benatan betza betzad hammecham venitgalgela chayyab umah shekkatab hambashshel bikli rosho "g deheebiro meal haesh chayyab haynu mishshum dezeh chashib mebashshel beor mammash ki hammecham vehaqqedera naasu hen atzman gachelet shel esh abal hahebel en bo mammashut veraq hu chom aviri veen hepresh ben hebel leben heashan degam hahebel hu ashan ella dehahebel chummo yoter chazaq vegadol min heashan mippene shekkanus betok betok hakkeli veeno mepushshat ak heashan hu mepushshat vehem inyan echad hem veraq shezzeh chummo yoter chazaq kemo shettomar yesh shekar veyesh spyrt"v verabbotenu za"l nistappequ baashan bishbil sheen bo mammashut ella hu chom aviri ukemo ken yippol hassapeq hazzeh behebel demay shena velaken kemo deqayma lan en bimushshan bishshule goyim ken haddin behammitbashshel behebel vezeh barur hare gam zehu taam nakon behetter hassoker hannizkar utemeheni al haggaon hamchabber ek dacha taam zeh bishte yadayim mikkoach din hammecham vehaqqedera dilpi dato yiqsheh leatzmo lamma nistappequ baggemara bamushshan vahalo chom heashan hu ba min haesh velamma en loqin bimushshan beissur shabbat veissur basar bechalab vahalo chom baashan shehu mebashshel ba lo min haesh vetzarik sheyyihyeh nechshab toledot haur kemo mecham uqedera hannizkarim leel ak beemet hattaam hu kemo shekkatabti bs"d deheashan en bo mammashut sheyyihyeh niddon kegachelet shel esh ukemo mecham uqedera vechummo asher mebashshel hu chom aviri vezeh hattaam yeshno gam behebel: beram mah shettaan lidchot shear taame hetter shekkatab harab morenu rabbi abraham yaaqob za"l haddin immo veyapeh taan veraq mah shettaan al taam acher sheamaro haggaon mehare"sh za"l vegam hu beatzmo chashab lomar ken barishona hinneh al taanato yesh lehashib veen kan maqom lehaarik veek sheyyihyeh beniddon hassoker hannizkar matzinu hetter barur "p hattaam shekkatabti dehave kan shelosha kochot veyoter veken yesh lo hetter barur "p hattaam shekkatab morenu rabbi abraham yaaqob za"l dehave kaggin hamushshan asher ana abeda asiti lo chizzuq vehimlatzti baado betub taam vedaat vehinneh ana abada asiti od hetter beniddon hassoker mikkoach sepeq sepeqa velo katabti kan bishbil leqatztzer haddebarim dilinyan dina en anachnu tzerikin lekak:

clarification.explanation:
Crystallized sugar made in Europe from red beets through cooking — the Gaon "Shem Aryeh" raised concern of "gentile cooking" here (since beets are not eaten raw except under difficulty, and even something eaten under difficulty carries the gentile-cooking prohibition), and was distressed at not finding a clear leniency for it. The Ben Ish Chai (in Rav Pe'alim) found a clear leniency for it, based on two main reasons:

(a) "Force of a force of his force" (three removes): the sugar is not cooked by the fire itself but by vapor. The gentile lights a fire and heats water — and from the water's heat vapor is born (this is already "the force of his force"), and the vapor rises through pipes and descends on its own into the vat containing the juice, cooking it slightly (a cooking not yet fit for eating), and from there to a second and third vat until the cooking is complete; and the gentile does not even handle the juice itself by hand, but it passes from vessel to vessel by machines (wheels). It follows that the cooking is done by "a force of a force of his force" (three removes or more). And we hold that "his force is like his body" regarding gentile cooking (like blowing with the mouth or a bellows — where the emerging air is considered like the force of his hand), but "the force of his force" does not forbid, and all the more so "a force of a force of his force." And even regarding wine used for idolatrous libation — where they were stricter, due to idolatry, such that even "the force of his force" forbids it — they permitted three removes after the fact (even for drinking); all the more so regarding gentile cooking, and in our case, which is in any event already "after the fact" (since the sugar is already made by gentiles) — it is entirely permitted.

He brought support from the law of the Sabbath in the Rambam: "his force" in a public domain the Sages forbade, "the force of his force" is permitted even in a public domain, and in a karmelit even "his force" is permitted. He raised a difficulty: one who blows on a fire is liable for "kindling" (since his force is like his body)! He resolved: all the labors of the Sabbath are derived from the Tabernacle — and blowing on a fire occurred in the Tabernacle (they blew to kindle), therefore "one who blows is liable"; but carrying from domain to domain in the Tabernacle was done by hand, not by force and throwing, therefore "his force" in carrying is not Torah-level but rabbinic (and only in a public domain), and in a karmelit (which is entirely rabbinic) they did not decree against "the force of his force"; and with wine they were stricter due to "a trace of idolatry."

(b) "Vapor is like smoke": the sugar is cooked only by vapor, and just as "there is no gentile-cooking prohibition in a smoked item" — since smoke has no substance but is only "airy heat," unlike a first vessel which itself becomes like an ember — so too something cooked by vapor, since vapor is like smoke (only its heat is stronger, since it is confined in a vessel). And although the Gaon "Shem Aryeh" firmly rejected the vapor reasoning, the Ben Ish Chai reconciled it: the kettle and pot are liable since they themselves become like an ember and have substance, unlike vapor (and smoke), which has no substance but only airy heat; and for this very reason our Sages were in doubt regarding a smoked item — showing it is the same law as vapor. Therefore, just as the Sages were in doubt about a smoked item because it has no substance, so is the law with vapor — and since they concluded "there is no gentile-cooking prohibition in a smoked item," so too with something cooked by vapor.

By both reasons — the sugar is permitted according to all opinions; and it has an additional leniency by force of a "double doubt."
takeaways: Sugar made from beets through cooking raised concern of gentile cooking, and the Ben Ish Chai found a clear leniency for it.

Reason one: the cooking is done by "a force of a force of his force" (vapor arriving through three removes) — which does not forbid under gentile cooking (even libation wine permits three removes after the fact, and here it is already after the fact).

Reason two: "vapor is like smoke," having no substance but only airy heat (unlike a kettle/pot, which become like embers) — and "there is no gentile-cooking prohibition in a smoked item"; combined with a "double doubt" — permitted according to all opinions.

paragraphs: Pat shemmannichin bo chatikot qetannot shel basar shemmearebin otam baqqemach beet hallisha veaach"k opin oto battannur kevan dachatikot basar ellu hem beayin betok happat hare ellu asurim mishshum bishshule goyim lepikak im haopeh shel yisrael hu goy sheopeh bebeto shel yisrael "g dehen osin hassaqa beyadam battannur kede lehattir happat. lo toil hassaqa zo bishbil habbasar sheyyesh bo issur bishshule goyim lekak tzarik sheyyadbiq hayisrael et happat zeh sheyyesh bo basar betannur deaz bazeh have kemo hannachat habbasar o haqqedera shekkatabnu leel bedin bishshule goyim:

clarification.explanation: Bread containing small pieces of meat, mixed into the flour during kneading and then baked in the oven — since the meat pieces are actually present within the bread, they are forbidden under gentile cooking. Therefore, if the baker is a gentile baking in a Jew's house, even though the household members do the firing themselves to validate the bread, this firing does not help for the meat inside it, since the meat has the law of gentile cooking, not bread. Therefore the Jew himself must attach this meat-containing bread to the oven, since this is then considered as though the Jew placed the meat on the fire himself.
takeaways: Bread with actual meat pieces inside — the meat is forbidden under gentile cooking.
Oven-firing validates the bread but not the meat inside it.
The Jew himself must attach such bread to the oven, considered as placing meat on the fire himself.

paragraphs: Kelim shebbishshel bahem haggoy dabar haasur bishshule goyim tzarik lahem heksher "y hagala vaapillu enam bene yoman asur lebashshel bahem lekattechilla ukemo shekkatab haggaon sipte daat besiman tz"g seip qatan g' dahalaka meruvvachat hi beyisrael daapillu issur derabbanan shennibla bikli la mehanne noten taam lipgam lekattechilla veayyen erek hashshulchan siman qy"g ot k"b veim hem kele cheres "g debishar issurin lo mehanne hagala likli cheres heqellu beissur bishshule goyim veameru magilo shelosha peamim vedayyo vaapillu im hem kele pirpuri yagilem shalosh peamim veraq im hem reuim sheyyodea hu sheim yagilem shalosh peamim berotechin paqei veikka hepsed merubbeh muttar lehishtammesh bahem achar k"d shaot belo hagala:

clarification.explanation: Vessels in which a gentile cooked something forbidden under gentile cooking require purging, and even if not within their day, it is forbidden to cook in them as the primary practice, since even a rabbinic prohibition absorbed in a vessel is not permitted as the primary practice by "imparting a spoiling taste." And if they are earthenware vessels, although purging does not help earthenware vessels for other prohibitions, for gentile cooking they were lenient and said purging three times suffices, and even fine porcelain vessels should be purged three times. Only if they are fragile, and one knows that purging them in boiling water would crack them, causing great loss, is it permitted to use them after twenty-four hours without purging.
takeaways: Vessels used by a gentile for gentile cooking require purging, even not within their day.
For gentile cooking, earthenware vessels need only triple purging, unlike other prohibitions.
Fine porcelain vessels are also purged three times.
Fragile vessels that would crack with great loss may be used after 24 hours without purging.

paragraphs: Im bishshel haggoy lecholeh beshabbat hattabshil asur lemotzae shabbat apillu lacholeh atzmo im yesh lo bishshul yisrael leekol vehakkelim tzerikin hagala v"g deyesh kan sepeq sepeqa veod sapeq shelishi name mikkol maqom kevan dehagala hu dabar naqel en lismok al sepeq sepeqa lehattir belo hagala "g dehu issur derabbanan abal kelim shel pirpure dehem keli sheni "g shehem chazaqim deim maggein la paqei mikkol maqom kevan demitqalqelim qetzat en tzarik lehagilam ella yishtammesh bahem achar k"d shaot:

clarification.explanation: If a gentile cooked a dish for a patient on the Sabbath, the dish is forbidden at the Sabbath's conclusion even to the patient himself, if he has a Jewish-cooked dish to eat, and the vessels require purging. And although there is here a double doubt plus an additional doubt for leniency, nevertheless, since purging is an easy matter, one should not rely on the doubts to permit it without purging, even though this is a rabbinic prohibition. But fine porcelain vessels, being a second vessel, even though they are sturdy and would not crack if purged, nevertheless, since they deteriorate slightly from purging, need not be purged, but should be used after twenty-four hours.
takeaways: A gentile-cooked dish for a patient on the Sabbath is forbidden at the Sabbath's conclusion if a Jewish-cooked dish is available.
The vessels require purging, since purging is easy and one should not rely on the doubts.
Fine porcelain vessels, which deteriorate from purging, need not be purged — use after twenty-four hours instead.

paragraphs: Kol shekar shel goyim hen shel temarim hen shel teenim hen shel seorim veshel tebua veshel debash aseru chaza"l mishshum chatnut velo aseru ella bimqom mekirato veqobea atzmo lishtot bebet haggoy abal im hebi hashshekar lebeto o shenniknas aray lebet haggoy lishtot veken im lan bebet haggoy hare zeh muttar lishtot be sheshshoteh mishshel baal habbayit ben sheshsholeach liqnot mimmaqom acher vekatab mvr"m za"l deyesh mattirin beshekar shel debash veshel tebua venahagu lehaqel bazeh yeuyyan sham vehammachmir gam bemaqom shennahagu hetter tabo alayv beraka:

clarification.explanation: All beer of gentiles — whether of dates, figs, barley, grain, or honey — the Sages forbade due to intermarriage. But they forbade it only at its place of sale, when one sets himself to drink at the gentile's house. But if one brought the beer to his own home, or entered a gentile's house incidentally to drink, and likewise if one lodges at a gentile's house, it is permitted to drink, whether drinking from the homeowner's own supply or bought elsewhere. The Rema wrote that some permit honey and grain beer, and the custom developed to be lenient about this. One who is stringent even where the lenient custom prevails is blessed.
takeaways: Gentile beer is forbidden due to intermarriage, but only at its place of sale when one sets himself to drink there.
Brought home, drunk incidentally, or while lodging there, it is permitted.
Some permit honey and grain beer, and the custom is lenient.
One who is stringent even where the lenient custom prevails is blessed.
